reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Presents with pain and tenderness over the radial styloid, aggravated by thumb and wrist movement and by gripping and lifting
It affects the first dorsal extensor compartment, involving abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis as they pass under the extensor retinaculum
It is commonly seen in new parents lifting infants and in occupations or activities with repetitive thumb use, and more often in women, especially postpartum
The Finkelstein test, reproducing pain when the thumb is flexed into the palm and the wrist ulnar-deviated, supports the diagnosis
The underlying pathology is thickening of the tendon sheath and stenosis of the compartment rather than a purely inflammatory tenosynovitis
First-line management is activity modification, a thumb spica splint, and analgesia by principle
Corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal compartment is effective for cases not settling with conservative measures
A separating septum within the compartment can reduce injection success and may need to be addressed surgically
Surgical release of the first dorsal compartment is reserved for refractory cases, protecting the superficial radial nerve
reference.pathophysiology: De Quervain tenosynovitis is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist. Repetitive or sustained thumb and wrist loading causes thickening and myxoid degeneration of the tendon sheath and retinaculum, narrowing the fibro-osseous tunnel through which abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis run. The resulting friction and impaired tendon gliding produce pain over the radial styloid.
additionalInvestigations: Usually a clinical diagnosis based on history and the Finkelstein test
Ultrasound to confirm thickening of the retinaculum and tendon sheath and to detect a septum
Plain radiographs if basal joint arthritis or a bony cause is suspected
MRI only in atypical or refractory cases
Assessment of the superficial radial nerve when nerve irritation is suspected
redFlags: Signs of infection such as warmth, spreading erythema, fever, or a penetrating injury
Neurological symptoms suggesting superficial radial nerve involvement
History of trauma raising concern for scaphoid or other fracture
Failure to respond to appropriate treatment, prompting diagnostic review
reference.prognosis: Most cases respond well to splinting and corticosteroid injection, and postpartum cases often settle as hormonal and mechanical factors resolve; a minority need surgical release, which is generally successful.
pitfalls: Confusing it with thumb basal joint arthritis, which needs different treatment
Injuring or overlooking the superficial radial nerve during injection or surgery
Failing to recognise a compartment septum causing injection failure
Neglecting activity modification so symptoms persist or recur
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Advise activity modification, avoiding provoking thumb and wrist movements, and immobilise in a thumb spica splint
Provide analgesia with oral or topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Offer corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal extensor compartment for persistent symptoms, which is often highly effective
Refer for hand therapy with tendon-gliding and graded strengthening as symptoms settle
Reassure postpartum patients that symptoms often resolve as hormonal and mechanical factors improve
Reserve surgical decompression by first dorsal compartment release for refractory cases, taking care to protect the superficial radial nerve

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of De Quervain tenosynovitis

nodes.text: Suspected de Quervain tenosynovitis: radial wrist pain worse with thumb movement
Red flag present (infection signs, nerve symptoms, or trauma suggesting scaphoid injury)?
Urgent: treat infection or investigate a suspected scaphoid fracture
Finkelstein test with history; ultrasound for sheath thickening or a septum
Does ultrasound confirm first dorsal compartment thickening?
Review basal joint arthritis, scaphoid pathology or superficial radial nerve entrapment
Splint and activity modification with NSAIDs for analgesia
Corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal extensor compartment
Hand therapy with tendon-gliding and graded strengthening
First dorsal compartment release for refractory cases; protect the nerve
Most settle with splinting and injection; surgery is generally successful
